column7: Gibson's Maestro timeline dates the FZ-1 Fuzz-Tone to 1962, making it one of the foundational commercial solid-state guitar effects.
column10: Treat 1962 as the builder-published introduction year; preserve later FZ-1 variants separately.

column7: Gary Hurst developed the original Tone Bender in 1965 after the commercial appearance of the Maestro Fuzz-Tone, with Macari/Sola Sound bringing the product to market in the UK.
column10: The earliest MKI enclosure was wedge-shaped; avoid over-precise first-batch dates.

column7: Early Tone Bender MKI production used a gold-and-black wedge-shaped steel enclosure, providing a strong external identification marker.
column10: Use enclosure shape and finish as specimen clues, not as a sole chronological proof.

column7: The MK1.5 emerged soon after the original Tone Bender and used a rounded sand-cast enclosure; this state is commonly called MK1.5 even though the case itself did not carry that designation.
column10: Preserve the community designation as a useful historical discriminator while noting that the original product labeling differed.

column7: The MK1.5 design was supplied in different branded forms, including Rotosound, and became the historical basis for later Italian Vox Tone Bender production.
column10: Keep OEM branding relational rather than treating every badge as a new family.

column7: The early Fuzz Face belongs to the same two-transistor historical branch as the Sola Sound MK1.5, with germanium production preceding and overlapping the later silicon transition.
column10: Use overlap windows rather than a fabricated single transition date.

column7: Sola Sound's Professional MKII was introduced in 1966 and became the major three-transistor Tone Bender platform supplied to multiple brands as an OEM product.
column10: Sola Sound itself is the builder/OEM; Vox, Marshall and Rotosound should remain distinct retail objects.

column7: Early Marshall Supa Fuzz examples were supplied by Sola Sound and belong to the Tone Bender MKII family; Marshall began its own manufacturing around 1968.
column10: Enclosure geometry can distinguish Sola Sound-supplied units from later Marshall-built production.

column7: Rotosound received Sola Sound's MKII-family fuzz design as an OEM-branded Fuzz Box during the 1966-1968 period.
column10: Preserve Rotosound as a retail/OEM object inside the MKII family.

column7: The MKIII introduced a different three-transistor Tone Bender state with a tone-control function and appeared across Sola Sound, Vox, Park and Rotosound branding.
column10: The added tone control is a strong external identification clue.

column7: The MKIV retained the MKIII-era product family while moving into a distinct smaller enclosure; MKIII and MKIV forms overlapped during the 1970s.
column10: Do not use enclosure change alone to imply a single exact production cutoff.

column7: Park Fuzz Sound examples appear in the 1969-era Sola Sound OEM network and use the Tone Bender MKIII family.
column10: Preserve Park as the retail brand and Sola Sound as the OEM lineage.

column6: Early Project V examples date to 1968, while the model is documented in WEM advertisements and catalog material from 1969; surviving examples provide useful physical dating evidence.
column9: Date codes alone are insufficient for an exact launch date; preserve 1968-1969 as the evidence-backed window.

column7: Mike Matthews and Bob Myer place the Big Muff's release in 1969, with early documentation advertising it in 1970; early examples are associated with the plain-metal Triangle enclosure.
column10: Preserve 1969 release claim and 1970 advertising evidence rather than forcing a single documentation date.

column7: Electro-Harmonix historical material identifies Muff Fuzz as an earlier dirt product sold in a compact LPB-1-style enclosure before the larger Big Muff Pi.
column10: Keep Muff Fuzz as a separate product family/precursor rather than treating it as a Big Muff enclosure variant.

column7: The earliest Big Muff examples are commonly identified by their triangular control layout and plain metallic enclosure before the larger graphic-era cases.
column10: Use control layout and enclosure together for specimen identification; exact serial cutoffs remain a separate research task.
